name: Refrigerator
blurb: A refrigerator's compressor cycles on and off, so its effective draw averages 100–250 watts around the clock. It's rarely the biggest item on a bill, but because it never turns off, an inefficient or failing fridge quietly costs more than most people expect.
tips: Vacuum the condenser coils yearly — dusty coils can add 10–25% to running cost.
Check the door gasket with a dollar bill; if it slides out easily, cold air is leaking constantly.
A second fridge in a hot garage can cost more than the kitchen one — consolidate if it's mostly empty.

name: Mini Fridge
blurb: Mini fridges average 40–100 watts of continuous draw. Per cubic foot they're actually less efficient than full-size refrigerators, so a dorm fridge kept for a few sodas can be a surprisingly poor deal.

name: Chest Freezer
blurb: Chest freezers are the most efficient cold-storage design — cold air stays put when you open the lid. A modern 9 cu ft unit often costs less per month to run than a mini fridge, though old units from the 1990s can cost three times as much.

name: Upright Freezer
blurb: Upright freezers trade some efficiency for convenience: cold air spills out of the vertical door each time it opens, and frost-free defrost cycles add consumption. Expect 20–40% higher running costs than an equivalent chest freezer.

name: Wine Cooler
blurb: Thermoelectric wine coolers run continuously and can use more electricity than a full-size refrigerator despite holding a fraction of the volume. Compressor-based models are meaningfully cheaper to operate.

name: Dishwasher
blurb: A dishwasher cycle uses roughly 1–1.5 kWh, most of it for heating water and drying. Running full loads on a normal cycle beats hand-washing on both water and energy for most households.
tips: Skip heated dry — air-dry or crack the door and save roughly a third of the cycle's energy.
Run full loads; a half-full cycle costs the same as a full one.
If your utility has time-of-use rates, the delay-start button is free money.

name: Electric Oven
blurb: Electric ovens draw 2–5 kW while heating, then cycle to hold temperature, averaging out to roughly 1.5–2.5 kWh for a typical hour of baking. Preheating is a minor cost; long roasts and self-clean cycles are the expensive events.

name: Electric Stove Burner
blurb: A typical electric coil or radiant burner draws 1,000–3,000 watts depending on size and setting. Day-to-day stovetop cooking usually lands mid-pack on a bill — well behind heating, cooling, and hot water.

name: Induction Cooktop
blurb: Induction transfers around 85–90% of its energy into the pan versus roughly 70–75% for radiant electric, so the same cooking finishes faster on fewer kilowatt-hours. It's the cheapest electric way to cook, and the gap widens for boiling-heavy cooking.

name: Microwave
blurb: Microwaves draw over a kilowatt but run in short bursts, so typical daily use amounts to a few cents. For reheating and small portions, the microwave is nearly always the cheapest cooking appliance in the kitchen.

name: Toaster
blurb: A two-slice toaster draws about 900 watts for two to three minutes — call it 0.03–0.05 kWh per use. Daily toast costs pennies per month everywhere in the country.

name: Toaster Oven
blurb: A toaster oven heats a small cavity with 1,200–1,800 watts, using one-third to one-half the energy of a full-size oven for small dishes. For anything that fits, it's the cheaper choice.

name: Air Fryer
blurb: Air fryers pull 1,400–1,800 watts but cook fast in a small basket, so a typical session uses about half the electricity of the same food in a big oven. Their real economy is short runtimes, not low wattage.
tips: Skip preheating for most foods — the small cavity comes to temperature almost immediately.
Batch-cook: two rounds back-to-back reuse heat the oven would have wasted.
For large trays that need two air-fryer batches, the big oven can break even.

name: Slow Cooker
blurb: A slow cooker sips 100–250 watts for six to eight hours, totaling roughly 0.7–1.5 kWh per meal — comparable to one hour of a full-size oven while being far gentler on a summer kitchen.

name: Electric Pressure Cooker (Instant Pot)
blurb: Electric pressure cookers heat hard for a short time, then hold pressure at low power — most meals finish under 0.5–0.8 kWh. They routinely beat both the stovetop and the oven for beans, stews, and rice-adjacent staples.

name: Rice Cooker
blurb: A standard rice cooker uses roughly 0.2–0.4 kWh per batch, then drops to a low keep-warm trickle. Left on keep-warm all day, though, that trickle can exceed the cooking energy itself.

name: Coffee Maker
blurb: Brewing a pot of drip coffee uses about 0.1–0.15 kWh. The hidden cost is the warming plate — leaving it on for two hours roughly doubles the energy of the brew itself, which is why thermal-carafe machines are cheaper to own.

name: Espresso Machine
blurb: Espresso machines draw 1,000–1,500 watts while heating, but shots are quick. The cost driver is idle time: prosumer machines left on to keep the boiler hot can use more energy idling than pulling shots.

name: Electric Kettle
blurb: An electric kettle is the most efficient way to boil water in an American kitchen — faster and cheaper than the stovetop for the same volume. A full 1.7 L boil runs about 0.1 kWh; boiling only what you need cuts that further.

name: Blender
blurb: Even high-powered blenders run for such short bursts that daily smoothies cost a few cents a month. Motor wattage here is about performance, not your electric bill.

name: Garbage Disposal
blurb: A disposal grinds for seconds at a time, adding up to mere minutes of runtime a month. Its electricity cost is effectively zero next to the water it runs with.

name: Range Hood
blurb: Range hood fans draw 60–300 watts depending on speed, plus lighting. An hour a day of venting lands in the pennies-per-week range — run it as long as cooking needs it.

name: Countertop Ice Maker
blurb: Portable ice makers cycle continuously while switched on, averaging around 100–150 watts — more than many refrigerators. Running one only on party days rather than around the clock changes its cost by an order of magnitude.

name: Deep Fryer
blurb: Countertop deep fryers hold oil at temperature with 1,200–1,800 watts, cycling the element once hot. A typical fry session uses roughly half a kilowatt-hour — the oil costs more than the electricity.

name: Electric Griddle
blurb: Electric griddles draw 1,000–1,800 watts across a large plate and cycle to hold temperature. A weekend pancake session costs a few cents — comparable to using two stove burners for the same time.

name: Waffle Maker
blurb: A waffle maker pulls about a kilowatt while heating its plates, and a full family batch uses under 0.2 kWh. This is breakfast-scale spending: cents, not dollars.

name: Bread Maker
blurb: A bread machine's full knead-rise-bake cycle uses about 0.4–0.6 kWh — noticeably less than baking the same loaf in a full-size oven, since the machine only heats a small insulated chamber.

name: Food Dehydrator
blurb: Dehydrators run low wattage for very long stretches — 8 to 24 hours per batch is normal — so a jerky run can quietly use several kilowatt-hours. Batch size and runtime, not rated watts, decide whether homemade dried food is a bargain.

name: Stand Mixer
blurb: Stand mixers rarely run more than a few minutes at a time, so even a powerful motor amounts to pennies per month of electricity. Buy for torque and durability, not energy ratings.
